screens.title: What is a Chaincode Package?
screens.narratorSegment: A chaincode package is a reproducible archive that wraps your smart contract source files together with a small metadata manifest. Think of it as a shipment crate: the source files are the contents and metadata. json is the shipping label that tells Fabric the chaincode language, import path, and other essential details. The standard archive format is. tar. gz, commonly named with a. tgz extension. Packaging enforces consistency: when each peer installs the same package, the computed hash and resulting chaincode ID will match. A concrete example is packaging a Go chaincode directory that contains your Go files and a go. mod file. If go. mod is missing, dependencies may be omitted and the package will not be reproducible. A common misconception is to treat packaging as optional file copy; in Fabric, binary equality of the package matters because the lifecycle uses the cryptographic hash to identify specific package contents. Key takeaway: packaging makes the chaincode verifiable, repeatable, and traceable across organizations. What is a Chaincode Package? means the .tgz plus metadata.json ensures identical package content across peers, enabling deterministic endorsement.. In practical terms, structure and purpose of the .tgz archive. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6 › Chapter 5.7 › Chaincode Package Definition
Definition
A .tgz archive containing your chaincode source plus a metadata manifest. It provides the deterministic input peers use to compute the package hash.
Contents
source files, module files (like go.mod), and metadata.json describing language and path.
Analogy
A shipping crate plus a label; the label tells Fabric how to interpret the contents.
Common mistake
Treating package as a simple copy of files — this breaks reproducibility and ID matching.
Example: package layout
myasset_chaincode/
  ├─ myasset.go
  ├─ go.mod
  └─ metadata.json

Packaged as: myasset_1.0.tgz
Key Takeaway
Ensure your chaincode root contains module files before packaging to avoid missing dependencies.

screens.title: Creating a Chaincode Package
screens.narratorSegment: Packaging is a single CLI step with a few mandatory flags that control output, language, path, and label. The primary command is the peer lifecycle chaincode package command. It accepts an output filename, the language of the chaincode such as golang, node, or java, the path to the chaincode source, and a label that you should use to encode the name and version. For example, for a Go chaincode in a directory named myasset_chaincode you would produce a package with a label like myasset_1.0. The label is human-readable and is later included in the chaincode ID, so choose it to support version management. A common pitfall is setting the --path incorrectly; always point to the chaincode root that includes required files like go. mod. Another pitfall is packaging without initializing the Go module, which can omit dependencies. After packaging confirm that the. tgz exists and contains metadata. json plus your source. This step is purely local and deterministic, so double-check before distribution. In practical terms, using peer lifecycle chaincode package with proper flags. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6 › Chapter 5.7 › Packaging Process
Packaging command anatomy
Required pieces: output filename, path to source, language, and label. The label should encode name and version to aid lifecycle tracking.
Checklist
  • Confirm go.mod exists for Go chaincode.
  • Set --path to the chaincode root directory.
  • Choose a descriptive --label like myasset_1.0.
Concrete example
peer lifecycle chaincode package myasset.tgz --path ./myasset_chaincode --lang golang --label myasset_1.0
After this runs you should see myasset.tgz in your working directory. Inspect it to confirm metadata.json and source files are present.

Labels and paths determine how the package is referenced later; double-check them now.

screens.title: Installing the Chaincode Package
screens.narratorSegment: Installing a packaged chaincode onto a peer is a local operation. The peer lifecycle chaincode install command takes the. tgz file and stores it on the peer's filesystem. Importantly, the peer computes a cryptographic hash of the package contents and combines that with your label to produce a Chaincode ID. The peer then reports this Chaincode ID in the install output. Recording that full identifier is crucial because subsequent lifecycle operations — approving a chaincode definition and committing it to a channel — require referencing this exact ID. A concrete example is running peer lifecycle chaincode install myasset. tgz and observing an output line that includes myasset_1.0:a1b2c3d4e5f6... A common misconception is that install activates the chaincode; it does not. Install simply makes the package available to the peer. Activation happens only after approval and commit at the channel level. Also remember that each organization that will endorse must install the same package locally so their computed IDs match. Installing the Chaincode Package means install stores the package on the peer and outputs a chaincode id made of label and package hash.. In practical terms, peer lifecycle chaincode install and what it does. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6 › Chapter 5.7 › Install Package
What install does
  • Stores the .tgz package locally on the peer.
  • Computes a cryptographic hash of the package contents.
  • Emits a Chaincode ID formed from label and hash for later lifecycle steps.
Example output
2023-10-27 ... Installed remotely: response:<status:200 payload:"
myasset_1.0:a1b2c3d4e5f67890abcdef1234567890deadbeef" >
Chaincode code package identifier: myasset_1.0:a1b2c3d4e5f67890abcdef1234567890deadbeef
Copy this Chaincode ID and keep it with your deployment notes; you will need it for approval and commit steps on your channel.

screens.title: Label vs Chaincode ID
screens.narratorSegment: Two identifiers appear during the chaincode lifecycle: the label you supply when packaging, and the chaincode ID produced by the peer upon installation. The label is a human-readable string you control — for example myasset_1.0 — and it helps you and your team track versions. The chaincode ID, however, includes that label but also appends a cryptographic hash derived from the package contents. This hash guarantees integrity: if any byte in the package differs, the hash changes and the chaincode ID will not match across peers. A practical example: two organizations package the same source but if one accidentally includes extra files, their computed chaincode IDs will differ and approval/commit steps will fail to align. A misconception is to assume the label alone is authoritative; labels are convenient but the hash portion of the chaincode ID is the source of truth for equality. Always record the full chaincode ID after install and compare across organizations before proceeding. Label vs Chaincode ID means always use the full chaincode id (label plus hash) for lifecycle commands to ensure exact package matching.. In practical terms, human labels versus cryptographic identifiers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Security Considerations during Packaging
screens.narratorSegment: Packaging and installing chaincode touches the supply chain of your blockchain applications, so security matters at every step. First, only package trusted source code and perform code reviews to detect vulnerabilities or malicious logic before you create an archive. Second, labels should be descriptive and unique to avoid version confusion; however the cryptographic hash is the true integrity check. Third, installing chaincode requires administrative privileges on the peer; restrict this operation to authorized administrators to prevent unauthorized deployments. Fourth, transfer of package files between environments should use secure channels and storage; do not rely on unencrypted file sharing for production packages. A concrete practice is to sign packages in your organization and to keep a deployment ledger that records who packaged and installed which label and ID. A common misconception is that packaging alone provides security; packaging only provides reproducibility and integrity via the hash — process controls and access controls are still required to protect the code supply chain. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Best practices
  • Code review and static analysis before packaging.
  • Restrict install to administrator identities.
  • Use secure channels when transferring .tgz files.

screens.title: Common Packaging and Installation Mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: There are a few recurring mistakes teams make when packaging and installing chaincode. First, missing module initialization for Go chaincode is frequent: if you forget go mod init and tidy, dependencies may not be recorded and the package will be incomplete. Fix: initialize the module and ensure go. mod is present before packaging. Second, incorrect --path makes the packaging tool include the wrong files or fail entirely; always package from the chaincode root or use the correct relative path. Third, failing to record the Chaincode ID after install leaves you unable to reference the installed package later; copy the ID to your deployment notes immediately. Fourth, assuming install activates the chaincode is incorrect; install only stores the package — approval and commit at the channel level activate it. A concrete troubleshooting tip: if two orgs report different chaincode IDs, compare package contents and metadata. json to find missing files or different labels. These checks will help you resolve most lifecycle packaging problems quickly. Common Packaging and Installation Mistakes means always initialize modules, verify paths, record the chaincode id, and remember install does not activate chaincode.. In practical terms, how to recognize and fix frequent errors. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

This ensures every endorsing peer runs exactly the same code, which is essential for deterministic transaction endorsement. We'll also cover the peer lifecycle commands used to create and install packages, what the chaincode ID represents, common mistakes like missing Go module setup or wrong paths, and security practices when moving packages between environments. Third, you'll execute peer lifecycle chaincode install correctly so peers store the package and return a cryptographic chaincode identifier. Fourth, you will reason about security implications such as ensuring trusted source code, appropriate labeling practice for versioning, and limiting installation to administrators. A chaincode package is a reproducible archive that wraps your smart contract source files together with a small metadata manifest. Think of it as a shipment crate: the source files are the contents and metadata. json is the shipping label that tells Fabric the chaincode language, import path, and other essential details. The standard archive format is. tar. gz, commonly named with a. tgz extension. Packaging enforces consistency: when each peer installs the same package, the computed hash and resulting chaincode ID will match. A concrete example is packaging a Go chaincode directory that contains your Go files and a go. mod file. If go. mod is missing, dependencies may be omitted and the package will not be reproducible. A common misconception is to treat packaging as optional file copy; in Fabric, binary equality of the package matters because the lifecycle uses the cryptographic hash to identify specific package contents.
